packages/govee/src/probe.ts.content: After `arm(true)` the probe has no try/finally, so the closing `arm(false)` is only reached on the happy path. If `user.confirmPaint(...)` rejects, `link.sendRaw(paint(...))` throws (e.g. `paint` raises RangeError when zones > 255), or `wait` rejects, the function exits without disarming and the unit is left with an open, live razer channel — a persistent device-state leak that survives the failed probe. Wrap everything after the arm in try/finally so the disarm is always written.

`attemptedZones` is clamped only from below. When `options.zones > 255`, `twoColourFrame` emits more than 255 zones and `paint()` throws `RangeError` (B0 nbSeg is one byte) inside the probe, which — combined with the missing try/finally above — aborts the probe mid-arm and never disarms. Clamp the candidate count to the protocol limit (1..255) before it is used.
packages/govee/src/probe.ts.suggestion_code:
// B0 nbSeg is one byte: clamp to the protocol limit so paint() cannot throw.
  const attemptedZones = Math.min(255, Math.max(1, Math.floor(options.zones)));

packages/govee/src/probe.ts.content: `next()` is not concurrency-safe: the read of `this.lastAt`, the `await wait(...)`, and the write of `this.lastAt` are not atomic. Two overlapping callers (e.g. the probe and an action sharing the per-device sequencer) both observe the same `lastAt` and then both send immediately, producing the back-to-back datagrams this class exists to prevent (the toolkit's third-datagram drop). Serialize calls through a chained promise/mutex so each `next()` waits for the previous one to finish before computing its spacing.

`readB2Status`/`readDevStatus`/`paceRetry` compute the deadline, RTT and pacing with raw `Date.now()`, ignoring the clock injected via `options.clock` and consumed by `CommandSequencer`. When a caller drives the probe with a fake/paced clock, the sequencer advances on fake time while these loops advance on wall time, so the resend cadence and the ≤ deadlineMs termination diverge and tests/qualification timing become non-deterministic. Thread an optional `clock` through `ReadbackOptions` and use it consistently for `started`, `sentAt` and `paceRetry`.

`devStatus` is only read when the B2 `status` reply failed to parse (`before.status !== null ? null : ...`). A reachable unit that answers `status` therefore reports `devStatusAnswered: false` even though it may well answer `devStatus`. This makes the recorded capability (and any UI/logic keyed on it) inaccurate for the common case. Read `devStatus` unconditionally (or track whether it was skipped rather than reporting a hard false).
packages/govee/src/probe.ts.existing_code: const devBefore = before.status !== null ? null : await readDevStatus(link, readOpts);

packages/govee/src/probe.ts.content: This `demonstration` text asserts a fact the probe never established: "the whole-fixture colorwc mode answered read-back on this unit". The probe never sends `colorwc` (and `devStatusCommand` is `devStatus`, not `colorwc`), and when `before.status !== null` the devStatus read-back is skipped entirely. The verdict therefore advertises a verified `colorwc` fallback that was not verified, which can send the failover down a transport that silently does nothing. Either actually probe the colorwc/devStatus read-back before claiming it, or reword the string to state the fallback is the protocol default and unverified.
packages/govee/src/probe.ts.suggestion_code: "the segmented channel is not verified and must not be streamed; use the whole-fixture colorwc mode as the default fallback",
packages/govee/src/probe.ts.existing_code: "the whole-fixture colorwc mode answered read-back on this unit, so it is the verified fallback; the segmented channel is not verified and must not be streamed",

packages/config/src/store.ts.content: `save()` overwrites the config file in place. If the process crashes, the disk fills, or another writer truncates mid-write, the file is left partially written; `readLayersFile()` then fails JSON.parse / schema validation and silently returns `null`, so ALL persisted config is discarded on next startup with no error or backup. Write to a temp file and rename atomically (rename is atomic on the same filesystem). Also note this call is uncaught: a write error (ENOSPC/EACCES) propagates out of `set`/`reset`/`importJson` AFTER the in-memory state and mirror were already mutated and the change was emitted, leaving memory and disk diverged.

`emit()` invokes listeners without isolation. A subscriber that throws aborts the loop, so later subscribers never receive the change; worse, in `set`/`reset`/`importJson` `emit()` runs BEFORE `this.save()`, so a throwing listener also skips persistence entirely, leaving the in-memory state changed but the file stale (change silently lost on restart). Wrap each listener call in try/catch (and/or move `save()` before `emit()`).

When `importPayloadSchema.safeParse` fails, `check.success` is false and `values` silently falls back to `{}`. Combined with `bad.length === 0`, the method returns `{ ok: true }` for malformed payloads that were never imported (e.g. `"hello"`, `42`, `{ "values": [1,2,3] }`), so callers believe the import succeeded while nothing changed. Return a failure when the schema does not match instead of coercing to an empty object.
packages/config/src/store.ts.suggestion_code:
if (!check.success) return { ok: false, badKeys: ["<invalid config payload: expected { version, values: object }>"] };
    const values = check.data.values ?? {};

packages/config/src/store.ts.content: `save()` rewrites the whole file from this instance's `mirror` with no lock and no read-merge-write. Multiple `PersistentConfigStore` instances can point at the same path (e.g. show-service always constructs one on `userData/config.json` and config-service falls back to constructing its own when `opts.store` is not passed), so each instance's `set/reset/load` clobbers the other's persisted changes (last-writer-wins), silently dropping data that the other instance still holds in its stale mirror. Consider a file lock or a read-merge-before-write, or enforce a single shared instance.

`load()` mutates the layers and mirror but never emits `config:changed`, so any subscriber (e.g. ConfigService's history, renderer caches) that has already subscribed keeps stale values when `load()` is invoked after construction. Additionally, keys whose `defineKey` throws are silently skipped, so renamed/unknown persisted overrides are dropped without any signal; and the surrounding `readLayersFile` returns `null` on any corruption, which is indistinguishable from an empty config. Consider emitting per-key changes and surfacing dropped keys.

packages/controller-flx4/src/backend.ts.content: Overlapping-poll / stop race. The interval callback fires `poll()` without awaiting it and without any in-flight guard, so a slow `listPorts`/`open` can overlap with the next tick. More seriously, there is no `stopped` flag: if `stop()` runs while a `poll()` is suspended on an await, the resumed `poll()` will fall through to `selectAndOpen()` and re-open the port, leaving the service `connected` (and leaking a new input) after teardown. Even in the connected branch, `this.input` becomes null during the await, so the comparison after `await` mis-detects a loss and emits a spurious `lost` status after stop. Serialize polls and add a stopped/generation guard checked after every await; also have `stop()` notify listeners.

Any error from `listPorts` is swallowed and coerced to an empty list, which the hotplug branch then interprets as "the controller port disappeared". A transient backend hiccup (driver busy, temporary failure) therefore produces a false `lost` transition, closes a still-valid input, and discards the real cause. Distinguish a real failure from an empty list (e.g. only treat it as loss when the call actually succeeded and the port is absent, otherwise surface the error).
packages/controller-flx4/src/backend.ts.existing_code: const ports = await this.driver.listPorts().catch(() => [] as Flx4PortInfo[]);

packages/controller-flx4/src/backend.ts.content: Same swallowing here: a failed `listPorts` becomes an empty list, so the backend is reported as `no input port matches ...` and the true error is lost. This can also mask a real port that exists, causing failover to a worse backend or a misleading `searching` state. Capture the error and report it in the attempt reason instead of silently converting to [].
packages/controller-flx4/src/backend.ts.existing_code: const ports = await driver.listPorts().catch(() => [] as Flx4PortInfo[]);

packages/controller-flx4/src/backend.ts.content: Native handle leak on open failure. `openPort` is called before any error handling; on Windows WinMM this is exactly the single-client case the file exists to report — `openPort` throws when another app holds the port and the freshly constructed `Input` is never closed, leaking a native RtMidi handle on every failed open attempt (which the hotplug poll repeats indefinitely). Wrap the construction/open/message-registration in try/catch and call `closePort()` on failure.

Failover state is misclassified. `lastUnavailable` is overwritten by every later probe/open failure, so the final `unavailable-on-this-device` classification reflects the *last* failure rather than a real "held by another client" condition. Consequences: (a) when all backends simply fail to load/probe (e.g. nothing installed), the service still reports `unavailable-on-this-device` instead of `failed`/`searching`; (b) on macOS a Windows-only probe failure can become the user-facing reason, so the remedy tells the user to install Windows MIDI Services. Also, if a port *was* matched but only the open failed, the `sawPort` branch is unreachable because `lastUnavailable` is set, so a genuinely openable-port failure is reported as a device-availability problem. Track availability separately from load/probe failures and prefer the `sawPort`→`failed` classification when a matching port existed.
packages/controller-flx4/src/backend.ts.existing_code: lastUnavailable = { reason: message, remedy: heldSingleClient ? WINDOWS_HELD_REMEDY : remedyFor(name) };

packages/controller-flx4/src/backend.ts.content: A single throwing event listener aborts delivery to the remaining listeners *and* propagates through the driver's message callback (`acceptBytes` is invoked directly from the backend's `onMessage`), which can disrupt the MIDI backend's read loop. Invoke listeners defensively (try/catch per listener) so one bad subscriber cannot break message delivery.
Same for status listeners: an exception from one subscriber prevents every subsequent listener from receiving the status update. Wrap each call in try/catch (or isolate per-listener).

Edge-case bug: `Array.prototype.slice(-0)` is equivalent to `slice(0)`, so `recent(0)` returns the *entire* buffer instead of an empty result. This affects `recentMessages`/`recentEvents` for any caller that passes 0. Guard for non-positive limits.

apps/desktop/src/routes/live/manual-inte.content: Clamp range [0.5, 2] is incompatible with the `master/intensity` request schema. `packages/ipc/src/index.ts:34` declares `value: z.number().min(0).max(1)`, and `ipc-router.ts:140` runs `channels[name].request.parse(payload)` before dispatch. Any sensitivity > 1 (e.g. `sensitivityIntent(9)` → 2, or the `sensitivityIntent(1.5)` used in the test) yields a value above the schema max, so `parse` throws a ZodError and the router returns `{ ok:false, error:{ code:'E_HANDLER' } }` — the control simply fails instead of applying intensity. Additionally, `Math.min/Math.max` propagate `NaN`, so a non-finite input yields `value: NaN` (also rejected by the schema) rather than a safe default. Clamp to the schema bounds and guard non-finite input.
apps/desktop/src/routes/live/manual-inte.suggestion_code:
const clamped = Number.isFinite(value) ? Math.min(1, Math.max(0, value)) : 0;
  return { channel: "master/intensity", payload: { version: 1, value: clamped } };
apps/desktop/src/routes/live/manual-inte.existing_code:
const clamped = Math.min(2, Math.max(0.5, value));
  return { channel: "master/intensity", payload: { version: 1, value: clamped } };

apps/desktop/src/routes/live/manual-inte.content: The `at` field is silently discarded, so the blinder is indistinguishable from a plain build. The `show/trigger-build` request schema (`packages/ipc/src/index.ts:64`) is `z.object({ version: v1 })` — there is no `at` — and zod's default object parsing strips unknown keys, so `at: nextPhraseBeat` never reaches the backend. The router handler `triggerBuild()` (`ipc-router.ts:43`) also takes no argument. Result: the "restraint-aware blinder carrying the next-phrase beat" advertised by the header comment is a no-op; the intended phrase-synced blinder fires as an immediate full build. If the blinder needs a distinct action/beat, it requires its own channel + schema (the `ManualChannel` union has no blinder/at-bearing channel today).
apps/desktop/src/routes/live/manual-inte.existing_code: return { channel: "show/trigger-build", payload: { version: 1, at: nextPhraseBeat } };

apps/desktop/src/routes/live/manual-inte.content: The `custom` flag never reaches the backend. The `venue/set-color` request schema (`packages/ipc/src/index.ts:80`) is `z.object({ version: v1, rgb: z.tuple([z.number(), z.number(), z.number()]) })` — no `custom` — and zod strips unknown keys during `request.parse`, so the "explicit custom free-colour opt-in" is a no-op and the handler `setVenueColor(req.rgb)` never sees it. Also, `rgb` is forwarded unvalidated: the schema only requires three `number`s, so floats, negatives, or values > 255 (and `NaN`) are accepted and forwarded to the driver. Add `custom` to the channel schema (or drop it here) and clamp/round rgb components to 0-255 integers.
apps/desktop/src/routes/live/manual-inte.existing_code: return { channel: "venue/set-color", payload: { version: 1, rgb, custom } };

apps/desktop/src/routes/live/manual-inte.content: Semantics of a momentary `flash` look inverted/unbalanced. `flashIntent(true)` maps to `master/resume` (run) and `flashIntent(false)` to `master/freeze` (persistent stop). A momentary flash control releasing to `master/freeze` would leave the master latched-frozen rather than releasing to the prior state, and the name "flash" does not match resume/freeze. Both payloads are individually schema-valid (`master/resume` `at: "bar"`, `master/freeze` `frozen: true`), so this is a behavioural/polarity concern rather than a schema error — confirm the intended on/off action before shipping.

Unknown section kinds silently resolve to white, masking contracts schema drift. If `@autolight/contracts` adds a new section kind (or the kind casing changes), `trackPalette` will quietly emit a white swatch with no signal that the `SWATCH_BY_KIND` map is out of date. Consider surfacing unmapped kinds (log/dev warning) so missing mappings are detectable.

packages/config/src/registry.ts.content: Malformed JSON defaults are silently swallowed. `defaultFor` catches `JSON.parse` failures and returns the raw string, so json-typed keys whose `defaultRaw` is not valid JSON yield a `string` instead of the promised object/array, with no error. Confirmed malformed payloads: `mixer.owner.factorWeights` (line 58, unquoted keys), `planner.sectionEnergy` (line 69, unquoted keys / `.3` literals), `analysis.bands` (line 113, unquoted keys), `govee.lan.interfaces` (line 130, `"[] (all eligible)"`) and `live.prolink.interfaces` (line 191, `"[] (all eligible)"`). Downstream consumers expecting objects/arrays will receive strings and fail silently or crash at a distance. Fix the registry payloads (e.g. quote JSON keys / drop the prose suffix) and make the parser fail loudly instead of returning a wrong-typed value.
packages/config/src/registry.ts.existing_code: if (def.type === "json") { try { return JSON.parse(def.defaultRaw); } catch { return def.defaultRaw; } }

packages/config/src/registry.ts.content: Wildcard/placeholder keys are registered as literal keys but are unusable. `defineKey` performs an exact `Map` lookup, so any concrete key under a pattern (e.g. `ui.shortcuts.blackout`, `qa.faults.cpu`, `govee.device.<fixtureId>.transportMode`) throws `unknown-config-key: ...`, even though the registry advertises these as configurable. Affected entries: `ui.shortcuts.*`, `qa.faults.*`, and both `govee.device.<fixtureId>.*` keys. Either implement prefix/parameterized matching in `defineKey`, or model these as pattern metadata separate from the resolvable key set so callers don't hit spurious `unknown-config-key` failures.
packages/config/src/registry.ts.existing_code: { key: "ui.shortcuts.*", type: "string", defaultRaw: "B blackout, W white, F freeze, A auto, M manual, Up and Down master, 1 to 9 presets", unit: "map", range: "", receipt: "spec 94", liveSafe: true, scope: "app" },

packages/config/src/registry.ts.content: `defaultsObject()` emits the literal pattern keys into the defaults object (e.g. `"ui.shortcuts.*"`, `"qa.faults.*"`, `"govee.device.<fixtureId>.transportMode"`) because `defaultFor` resolves them via the exact-match `byKey` map. These are not real config keys and will pollute every materialized defaults snapshot, producing spurious entries and masking the fact that no concrete sub-keys were materialized. Skip pattern keys (or expand them) when building the defaults object.
packages/config/src/registry.ts.existing_code: for (const k of KEYS) out[k.key] = defaultFor(k.key);

packages/config/src/registry.ts.content: Declared `type` contradicts `defaultRaw` semantics. `analysis.ml.offlineOnly` is typed `string` with `unit: "bool"` and a non-boolean default, so `defaultFor` returns a string that callers will compare/negate incorrectly. The same mismatch applies to `govee.lan.stream.keepaliveMs` (typed `string`, value `"0 (off)"` while consumers treat it as `0` = disabled) and `govee.ble.colorQuantizeLevels` (typed `string`, value `"0 (off)"`, unit "levels per channel"). Align `type` and `defaultRaw` (use `boolean`/`number` with a sentinel like `0`/`false` and document the "off" meaning) so `defaultFor` returns the type consumers expect.
packages/config/src/registry.ts.existing_code: { key: "analysis.ml.offlineOnly", type: "string", defaultRaw: "true during Live", unit: "bool", range: "", receipt: "spec 110", liveSafe: false, scope: "app" },

packages/config/src/registry.ts.content: No invariant enforcement when building the lookup. A duplicated `key` in `KEYS` would silently overwrite the earlier entry in `byKey` (and the earlier default in `defaultsObject`), and the header's stated "240 keys" invariant is never validated at load time. Add a build-time assertion that fails on duplicate keys and verifies the expected key count so registry drift is caught immediately rather than at runtime.

`defaultsSchema` validates nothing: `z.record(z.string(), z.unknown())` accepts any object shape, so none of the type/default mismatches in this registry (malformed json payloads, string-typed boolean/number keys) are detected. If this schema is meant to guard resolved config, derive it from `KEYS` (per-key validators with correct types and defaults) so invalid values are rejected instead of passing through silently.

packages/config/src/secrets.ts.content:
Data-loss bug in `flush()`: the persisted blob is rebuilt exclusively from `this.memory`, so any persistent id that is on disk but not currently loaded into memory is silently dropped, and if the resulting map is empty the whole blob is wiped via `clearBlob()`.

Concrete failure: a vault whose blob contains `govee.cloud.apiKey` and whose memory is empty (no `get`/`presence` call yet this session) receives `set("agent.apiToken", token)` (a MEMORY_ONLY id) or `remove("agent.apiToken")`. `persist` ends up empty, so `clearBlob()` erases the stored Govee key. A later `get("govee.cloud.apiKey")` returns `null` even though the user had stored it. The same structure breaks whenever more persistent ids are added: a `set` of one id overwrites the blob with only the ids currently in memory.

Fix: merge with the decrypted on-disk blob and only drop ids explicitly removed (e.g., track a `removed` set), instead of deriving disk state solely from live memory.

Two problems here:
1) `set()` mutates `this.memory` *before* `flush()` can throw. In degraded mode (`isEncryptionAvailable()` false, e.g. no OS keychain), `set("govee.cloud.apiKey", v)` throws from `flush()`, but the value stays in memory — so `get()`/`has()`/`presence()` report it as "stored" even though the caller was told the write failed. Worse, that retained persistent value makes every later `set("agent.apiToken", ...)`/`remove(...)` throw again (`persist` is non-empty), so the memory-only token can never be set.
2) `flush()` runs unconditionally even for MEMORY_ONLY ids, causing a needless disk write for the agent token and tying its success/failure to unrelated persistent state.

Validate encryption availability before mutating memory, and only persist when a persistent id actually changed.

Silent failure: any `decryptString`/JSON parse error is swallowed and reported identically to "not set". A corrupt blob or a keychain/OS-account mismatch therefore shows the key as `missing` in Settings, and the next `set()` silently overwrites the unrecoverable ciphertext (see the `flush()`/`clearBlob()` path), destroying the last chance to recover it. At minimum distinguish "unreadable" from "absent" (log/return a diagnostic) so corruption is not masked as an unset secret.

Sequential `split`/`join` replacement leaks part of a secret when one secret is a substring of another: with `secrets = ["abc", "abcdef"]`, replacing `"abc"` first turns `"abcdef"` into `"[redacted]def"`, then the `"abcdef"` pass matches nothing, leaving `def` in the output. This helper is the guard that keeps secrets out of logs/exports/crash reports, so a partial leak is a real exposure. Sort secrets by descending length (and de-duplicate) before redacting.

`toBase64`/`fromBase64` rely on the browser globals `btoa`/`atob`. This module deliberately avoids importing Electron to stay unit-testable, so it may be loaded in a Node/main context where these globals are absent (older Node/runtimes). When missing, `fromBase64` throws inside `get()` → swallowed by the catch → silently reported as "not set", while `toBase64` throws out of `flush()` → hard failure on every write. Use a runtime-agnostic base64 codec (e.g. `Buffer` when available, or feature-detect `btoa`) instead of assuming the globals exist.

The secret id list is duplicated across four places (`SECRET_IDS`, `SECRET_TABLE`, `MEMORY_ONLY_TABLE`, and these hardcoded keys in `presence()`). Adding a new secret requires editing all of them; forgetting `SECRET_TABLE` makes `isSecretId` reject the new id, and forgetting `presence()` silently hides it from Settings/diagnostics. Derive `SECRET_TABLE`/`MEMORY_ONLY_TABLE` and build `presence()` by iterating `SECRET_IDS` so the id set has a single source of truth.

packages/rekordbox-live/src/osc.ts.content: The top-level header pre-read runs outside the visitor's try/catch, so any datagram of >=8 bytes that does not contain a NUL within the buffer (e.g. `Uint8Array(8) {0x01,...}` with no 0x00, or a 4-7 byte NUL-terminated string whose 4-byte padding overruns) makes `readPaddedString` throw `RangeError("unterminated OSC string")` directly out of `decodeOscDatagram`. This violates the documented contract ("Malformed elements are reported, never thrown at the caller (S26)") and, since the only caller `ingestDatagram` (rkbx-osc.ts:193) does not wrap the call, an attacker can crash the caller with a single malformed UDP packet. The `bytes.length < 8` branch pushes the error into `malformed`, so the behavior is inconsistent between short and long un-terminated inputs. Prefer eliminating this duplicate read (see the unused `timetag` below) or at minimum wrap it in try/catch and push to `malformed`.

The 4-byte blob length prefix is bounds-checked, but the blob payload/padding is not: `at + 4 + len` is never validated against `data.length`. When `len` overruns the buffer, `data.slice()` silently truncates the blob and `at` is advanced past the end of the datagram, so the remaining args are no longer parsed at the correct offsets and the element is NOT reported in `malformed` — corrupting the parse instead of rejecting it. Validate the full padded length before slicing.

The bundle element loop condition `at + 4 <= data.length` silently ignores any residual 1-3 bytes left in the bundle (or a size prefix that cannot be fully read). A structurally malformed bundle is therefore accepted and reported as clean rather than added to `malformed`. After the loop, flag any leftover bytes.

`timetag` is read here but never used inside `visit` (the return value for the top level is recomputed separately at the end of `decodeOscDatagram`). This is dead code and is the root cause of the duplicated `#bundle`/timetag parsing; remove it (or have `visit` return the top-level timetag so the header is parsed only once).

Integers outside the int32 range fall through to the `f` (float32) branch, so e.g. `args: [5_000_000_001]` is encoded as a float tag, silently losing precision and round-tripping to a non-integer. Consider throwing for out-of-range integer arguments (or documenting the fallback) rather than emitting a precise-looking but lossy float32.
